In accordance with Figure 7, pressurized housings for all motors must be purged with air to meet the Class 1, Zone 2 hazard requirements for the dispenser. Additionally, an e-stop button was added for additional safety compliance. Figure 17. Robotic hydrogen dispenser equipped with tubing for both hydrogen and air purge. The camera for locating the robot to the fuel cell was found to be blocked by the additions of the flexible gas tubing. The camera targets on the fuel cell were repositioned for better sight lines by the robot camera. This change enabled proper positioning of the nozzle to the receptacle and fewer errors stopping the robot during positioning while testing with a fake fuel cell front plate (Figure 18). The first completed items were fine tuning the robot to target positioning to account for the new target positions on a real fuel cell (Figure 19). Shoulder motor over current errors limited the robot from getting to the fully inserted position to achieve a latch on a real system. Plug optimized the robot, locator tag (bar codes), and nozzle location to get the best results for the robot. The challenge for this robot is the location of the locator tag to the nozzle location needs to be very precise because this camera does not “see” the nozzle, only the locator tag. This approach is a limitation for production systems. With the location correct within 0.25mm the robot could approach the receptacle reliably. Even with a precise location, the robot did not have enough force to fully engage the nozzle onto the receptacle and latch. Now the robot is in a real-world environment with the H2 hose supported by the robot chassis, air hosing to allow H2 purging of the motors, and connecting to a real system. The robot approaches the nozzle and starts the insertion, but robot cannot push the last 3-6 mm to get to the latch position. Many work arounds were tried including re-mounting the H2 hoses and air hoses, trying to drive the robot deeper (with the locator to nozzle position deeper in the robot software), and by “helping” the robot the final distance. Ultimately only helping the robot drive the final distance worked to allow the robot to latch onto the H receptacle. 2 Plug proceeded to attempt the 200 connection cycles by “helping” the robot. Unfortunately, the pulling of the robot during insertion lead to a gradual increase in robot positional errors. The best outcome was 10 successful insertions before the robot could no longer approach the receptacle properly. The worst was 2 successful insertions. Over 1.5 hours of testing Plug completed 29 successful latches with an average number of successful latches of 4 before failure. Data from these latches was captured and video taken as well.
